lesson.title: The Off Switch: How End Products Shut Down Their Own Pathway
lesson.summary: Feedback inhibition occurs when a pathway's final product allosterically inhibits the first enzyme in that same pathway, letting the cell automatically stop production once enough product has accumulated.
lesson.body:
Metabolic pathways are assembly lines: one enzyme converts a starting molecule into an intermediate, a second enzyme converts that intermediate into another, and so on until a final product emerges. Left unchecked, a fast running assembly line would keep consuming raw materials and energy long after the cell has enough of the final product. Feedback inhibition solves that problem by letting the end product of a pathway act as an allosteric inhibitor of an enzyme earlier in that same pathway, usually the very first enzyme, so the pathway shuts itself off once it has made enough.

This is allosteric regulation applied with a specific logic. The end product does not resemble the early substrate closely enough to be a competitive inhibitor at the active site; instead, it binds an allosteric site on the first enzyme and reshapes it so substrate can no longer bind well. As the product accumulates, more enzyme molecules get switched off and flux through the pathway slows. As the cell uses up the product, the inhibitor concentration drops, the enzyme relaxes back into its active shape, and the pathway resumes. The system self corrects without any outside signal or genetic change.

A well studied example is bacterial isoleucine synthesis, a five step pathway that converts the amino acid threonine into isoleucine. Isoleucine, the final product, allosterically inhibits threonine deaminase, the enzyme that catalyzes the very first step of its own synthesis pathway. When isoleucine is abundant, it binds threonine deaminase and shuts the pathway down; when isoleucine runs low, the inhibition lifts and the cell resumes making it. The cell never wastes threonine, energy, or the four other enzymes' worth of catalytic effort producing an amino acid it does not currently need.

Regulating the first step of a pathway, often called the committed step because it is the point of no easy return into other uses for the starting material, is efficient for a specific reason: shutting down that one early enzyme prevents the buildup of every intermediate downstream of it, not just the final product. If a cell instead regulated only the last enzyme in the chain, all the earlier intermediates would still accumulate uselessly. Targeting the first, committed enzyme lets one allosteric switch control the output of the entire multi enzyme pathway.

Feedback inhibition shows up throughout metabolism, from amino acid and nucleotide synthesis to cholesterol production, and it is one of the main reasons cells can maintain stable internal concentrations of thousands of different molecules simultaneously without constant outside instruction. It is fast, because it relies on existing enzyme molecules changing shape rather than making or destroying proteins, and it is self limiting, because the inhibitor's own concentration is what determines how strongly the brake is applied.
